data.content_ref: inline:The dependence claim asserts that without the lineage-dependency tax there is no cost asymmetry between within-basin descent and cross-basin exploration, but this conflates an institutional allocation cost with the intrinsic topological cost of escaping a basin. The refutation clause is actually satisfied by the target's own framing: saddle-crossing costs are a function of the loss-landscape geometry (basin depth, barrier height), which is a property of the problem space, not of the ownership regime. A lineage tax may *amplify* the asymmetry, but the target provides no mechanism showing it is the *sole* or *necessary* source of directed bias—rival lineages could face different saddle heights due to epistemic landscape structure alone (e.g., one basin is deeper because it captures more evidence), yielding directed suppression without any lineage-dependency tax at all.
